replying_to: Replying to Cascaded Fast and Slow Models for Efficient Semantic Code Search
display_title: Official Review of Paper2469 by Reviewer cXHD

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper focuses on the code samples retrieval problem that can be used to improve code reachability inside organizations - given a set of the code samples, retrieve the ones which are relevant to a text description of the code. Authors argue that the task has a reasonable value for practical applications. 
Paper discusses improvement of technical details over the previous works, like longer training/bigger batch etc and employ cascaded approach based on the 1) embedding of code samples into a constant vector space and retrieving top-K elements which are closest to the query; 2) re-rank the retrieved elements using a heavy ranker, which is typical for most practical information retrieval solutions.
Studied solution gives better performance on the CodeSearchNet dataset exhibiting higher metrics compared to previously reported numbers as well as reasonable latency.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
Paper is clearly written, provides a seemingly reasonable solution for the code search problems and shows improvement over the previously reported results. I guess it might be interesting for those who build practical code search systems.

Weaknesses:
The main weakness with the paper is lack of context from general information retrieval works as the problem is very similar. There are production-ready solutions that can do the same two proposed steps (and overall the concept of candidate generation and heavy ranking is very old and used ) and even more, e.g. late fusion between query and the candidate items [arxiv 2004.12832]. I would point to the vespa's blogpost discussion of an already working production solution https://blog.vespa.ai/pretrained-transformer-language-models-for-search-part-1/ 

It also not very clear what is the performance of the slow part of the proposed encoder alone (applied to the whole corpus). There is a plot in Fig. 4, but it is hard to read only only up to 6K samples. It is not clear if the observed bump in metrics for heavy classifier is due to filtering from the fast encoder or due to a better heavy classifier.

From a minor point, it would be nice to add actual time in Fig. 2, so the reader can understand what is the improvement without looking in the table.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper lacks comparison/context from the information retrieval and the proposed solutions with fast candidate generation and heavy transformer-based re-ranking that are now available as out-of-the-box production systems.
I think that after adding the information retrieval context the paper might fit to more specialized or practical conferences, but lack of novelty makes it hard to recommend for ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their comments and feedback. Please find our response to the same below.

Re: Lack of context

We agree that adding context from the information retrieval domain can help the completeness of our paper. Thank you for pointing out the resourceful blogpost on this topic. We attempted ideas along late fusion for the problem of semantic code search but these did not give any significant improvements over the fast encoder baseline (mentioned briefly in Sec 5).. 

Re: performance of the slow part of the proposed encoder alone (applied to the whole corpus) 

Using the slow part over the whole corpus (all candidates x all validation set queries) is extremely computationally expensive for all the 6 programming languages. Hence we only report its performance over a set of K candidates selected in the first stage, with K less than 10,000. As the recall from the first stage is very close to 1 for K >= 1000 for all the 6 PLs (Fig. 5), we don’t expect the slow stage’s performance over the whole corpus (K = |C|) to be significantly better than the best performance reported in Fig 4. 

Re: It is not clear if the observed bump in metrics for heavy classifier is due to filtering from the fast encoder or due to a better heavy classifier.

The observed improvement can be primarily attributed to the slow classifier, however to make the use of this model computationally feasible the fast encoder stage plays a very important role of extracting the top K candidates.

content.title: Re: Response to Reviewer 4
content.comment:
Thank you for your response!

>We agree that adding context from the information retrieval domain can help the completeness of our paper. Thank you for pointing out the resourceful blogpost on this topic. We attempted ideas along late fusion for the problem of semantic code search but these did not give any significant improvements over the fast encoder baseline (mentioned briefly in Sec 5)..

I've noticed that you've mentioned a fusion mechanism. I guess it makes sense that it didn’t help much, since you have a shared architecture and when you run the slow classifier the candidate is passed through the same neural network that generated the embeddings, not adding much new information.

I suspect using other approaches such as colbert should provide a bigger difference. It helped enough for the general setting to become a standard, and the general setting is known to generalize well (e.g. text-to-image search)


>we don’t expect the slow stage’s performance over the whole corpus (K = |C|) to be significantly better than the best performance reported in Fig 4.

For the performance of the slow part, I suspect that it might even degrade when the K is big. That can be seen in Fig. 4 - for many languages it starts decreasing with K. This can happen because you have different losses for slow and fast parts - the fast part can train with way more negatives (up to the whole corpus) and thus have better generalization for “obvious” negatives.

I think it would be nice to see the attribution for the observed gains - compare how the fast encoder affects performance of the separately trained slow classifier (I thought that some of the baselines are the slow classifiers). Probably using a smaller subset of the queries or doing an experiment on a single language would be enough to see the difference, though that it up to the author's discretion as I do not think it is the main weakness of the paper

display_title: Official Review of Paper2469 by Reviewer PcBf

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper contributes an approach for retrieving semantically relevant programming code, in response to a natural language query. The approach consists of a jointly trained transformer encoder (to retrieve from the index) and a re-ranking component (to improve top-k performance). The authors find improvements over SOTA baselines in terms of effectiveness (MRR, recall) and efficiency (runtime approximations).
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- The experiments use known SOTA baselines and a benchmark dataset that is available to the community. 
- The components of the architecture are also known to the community and described in a way that can be, within reason, approximately reproduced.
- There is clear motivation for the task of searching programming code, and also for the specific architecture used in this work.
- The paper is overall clearly & coherently written.


Weaknesses:
- In section 3, the authors state that when using a transformer, the interactions between the natural language (NL) and programming language (PL) tokens in the self-attention layers can help improve the precision of the authors' approach of jointly encoding NL & PL, as opposed to encoding them independently. It is well known however that self-attention in transformers is in fact more messy than that. For instance, while some heads learn to assume indeed salient roles, other heads learn to assume non salient roles and can be pruned as redundant without impacting performance, while other heads, when pruned, can even lead to improved effectiveness (indicating potential noise in their learned roles). See Michel et al. NeurIPS 2019 and Voita et al. ACL 2019, for example. 

- In section 4, the authors state that they use a version of the CodeSearchNet code corpus that has been previously used by Guo et al. 2021, where low-quality queries are filtered out and the retrieval set is expanded, so that the corpus is more challenging and realistic. Removing low-quality queries renders a dataset neither more challenging, nor more realistic. Quite the opposite.

- In section 4, the two effectiveness evaluation measures used are MRR and recall@K. MRR considers only the rank of the first relevant retrieved item, which means that it is created for search tasks where we only care about the first correct answer. It is not argued in the paper why code search as a task should be evaluated with this measure precisely. It is not clear that code search is a single-hit type of retrieval task. I understand that prior work has also used this measure and that re-use of it facilitates comparison to prior work (which I agree with). However, the driving force for choosing an evaluation measure should be its fit to the task. This should be argued in the paper, because it is not self-evident. The second evaluation measure, recall@K, is defined as the number of retrieved items in the top K divided by the total number of relevant items in the corpus. Recall@K assumes that all relevant items, for each query, have been identified in the corpus. It is not clear if this is the case or not here. Is the whole corpus (including its modification by Gun et al.) exhaustively annotated for relevance? Finally, the combination of MRR and recall@K as the two sole evaluation measures of effectiveness is not optimal. On one hand, MRR disregards any relevant items (their number and their ranking) except the single top retrieved relevant item. On the other hand, recall@K ignores the rank position of retrieved relevant items, and just considers their number within the top K (i.e. recall treats the ranking as a set). Ranking is an important quality in search, which is why so many ranking-based evaluation measures are used to measure search effectiveness (e.g. NDCG, MAP, bPREF, etc.). 

- In Table 3, some missing SOTA baselines are GPT-C by Svyatkovskiy et al. 2020 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2005.08025.pdf and C-BERT by Buratti et al. 2020 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.12641.pdf.

- Are the results reported in Section 4 the average over several runs? More details should be provided. Also, no statistical significance test results are reported. This should be amended.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work is interesting in itself. The topic is timely and has merit. The experimental evaluation is somehow limited, in the choice of evaluation measures, lack of statistical significance testing, choice of baselines, and lack of precise details about some testing methodologies. Overall, it is not enough to run experiments and report scores. Scores should be analysed to make sure they are indeed indicative of the claims made in the paper. There is not much experimental analysis of that type in the paper or in the appendix.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their feedback and suggestions on improving the draft. Please find our responses below.

Weakness 1: Our argument was based on the comparison between the fast and slow models - the fast one encodes the NL and PL sequences independently, while the slow model encodes them jointly. While we don’t offer concrete proof as to why the joint encoding approach does a better job than independent encodings at the task of semantic search, our intuition is based on previous works handling bimodal data in similar settings (Miech et al, CVPR 2021). Nevertheless we agree that this can be further clarified in the paper to avoid readers from drawing any oversimplifications.

Weakness 2: We apologise for the confusion caused here. We agree, removing low quality queries will not lead to a challenging or realistic scenario. Using a larger retrieval set is what would lead to a more challenging or realistic setup. 

Weakness 3: Thanks for pointing this out. We agree that our choice of evaluation metrics warrants a discussion in the paper.

Re: Recall@K assumes that all relevant items, for each query, have been identified in the corpus. It is not clear if this is the case or not here. 
For test and validation set queries, we only have a single relevant item in the retrieval corpus/set. Recall@K for a single query can therefore be 0 (correct code snippet retrieved in top-K results) or 1 (correct code snippet retrieved in the top-K results).

Re: Is the whole corpus exhaustively annotated for relevance?
The annotation exists in the form of bimodal pairs (pairing/1-1 mapping of a docstring with a code snippet) for all training, test and validation queries.

Weakness 4: To the best of our knowledge, the model checkpoint for GPT-C and C-BERT are not yet released publicly. Besides, the two works study a different set of programming language tasks like AST node tagging, vulnerability identification and code generation/completion and adapting them for code search would be possible but non trivial.

Weakness 5: Given the expensive nature of these experiments (eg. 400+ GPU hours for training the Php shared model) we were able to report the results for a single run only.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2469 by Reviewer wD3o

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, the authors propose a cascaded approach of semantic code search based on establishing fast and slow models. A transformer encoder model first creates an index for fast retrieval, and a classification-based reranker fine-tunes the top rankings. Experiments are conducted on six datasets of different programming languages. The experimental results show that the proposed method outperforms several baseline methods.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

* The transformer-based encoder models both natural language and programming language, thereby providing the foundation for indexing and classification-based re-ranker.

* The fast encoder efficiently filters out irrelevant candidates so that the re-ranker can focus on the ones that are more relevant. 

* Publicly available datasets for reproducibility.

Weakness:

* The idea of using a fast retriever to select limited candidates for reranking is not novel. Especially in the field of deep learning of ad-hoc retrieval, it is almost impossible to use the ultimate deep models to derive relevance scores over the whole corpus.

* The description of the method is unclear. Lots of the details are missing, such as how to derive KNNs and essential hyper-parameters.

* The experimental setup is also unclear. For example, how the slow classifier (and the ones without pre-filtering) derive the final ranking?

*  The writing also needs to be polished. There are several grammatical errors and formatting issues.
content.summary_of_the_review: Due to the limited novelty and unsatisfactory quality of description and writing, I would recommend "5: marginally below the acceptance threshold".

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their careful reading and providing feedback. Please find our responses below.

Re: The idea of using a fast retriever to select limited candidates for reranking is not novel. Especially in the field of deep learning of ad-hoc retrieval, it is almost impossible to use the ultimate deep models to derive relevance scores over the whole corpus.

We agree with your remark on the extensive use of these hybrid approaches in text retrieval. In our case however, we show the applicability of these cascaded models across the modality of natural and programming language. 

Re: The description of the method is unclear. Lots of the details are missing, such as how to derive KNNs and essential hyper-parameters.

We study the impact of K on metrics like recall and MRR values of the fast encoders (Fig 4 and 5). This guided our choice of K. Besides batch-size, other hyperparameters in training the fast encoders are kept identical to prior work, with details in the appendix (batch size, learning rate, optimizer, loss functions formulation). We’d appreciate more feedback on what additional details could help the completeness of our paper.

Re: The experimental setup is also unclear. For example, how the slow classifier (and the ones without pre-filtering) derive the final ranking?

For each query-candidate pair, the slow classifier returns the probability of the candidate being the right response to the query. For a candidate set of size C, we then have C probability values which we can sort to get a ranking of the candidates. As one can imagine, this requires C forward passes and is therefore a slow method without the filtering from the first stage. We’d appreciate it if you could point out more areas where we could improve upon in terms of clarity.

display_title: Official Review of Paper2469 by Reviewer DPco

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work addresses the problem of efficient semantic code search where the database consists of code snippets and the queries are in natural language. It proposes a hybrid approach that ranks code snippets in two stages where in the first stage a fast retrieval model is employed to retrieve a small set of candidates from the database which are reranked in the second stage using a slow classification model. Such a hybrid approach would naturally give a trade-off between query response time and retrieval efficacy that might be desirable when either the fast retrieval model in itself is not very effective and the slow classification model is too slow to be useful on its own.
content.main_review:
This work addresses the problem of efficient semantic code search where the database consists of code snippets and the queries are in natural language. Tools that provide such a search feature can potentially be useful in increasing the productivity in software development by allowing reuse or repurposing of existing code snippets. 

Existing solutions to the problem of semantic search either use relatively less effective but fast retrieval models or somewhat more effective but slow classification models. The current work proposes a hybrid approach that ranks code snippets in two stages where in the first stage a fast retrieval model is employed to retrieve a small set of candidates from the database which are reranked in the second stage using a slow classification model. Such a hybrid approach would naturally give a trade-off between query response time and retrieval efficacy that might be desirable when either the fast retrieval model in itself is not very effective and the slow classification model is too slow to be useful on its own.

However, the idea of using a two stage approach to retrieval ranking is not new. It is a fairly old and well-worn technique in Information Retrieval literature. See, for e.g., [1] for an application of this technique in the area of Natural Language Processing. 

In order that the hybrid approach give the desired trade-off between query response time and retrieval efficacy, it is necessary that the first stage involving the fast retrieval model has very high recall (but not necessarily very high precision) and the second stage involving the slow classification model has very high precision. The current work ensures the first by making use of a competent fast retrieval model and also the second through a competent classification model. Both the fast retrieval model (encoder) and the slow classification model (classifier) make use of Transformer architecture. A contrastive loss, infoNCE, is used in the training of the encoder whereas cross-entropy loss is used in the in the training of the classifier. Both make use of bimodal dataset consisting of positive pairs and negative pairs.

One consequence of using two different models in a hybrid approach such as the one proposed in the current work is that the memory footprint of the models is substantially increased. This issue has a trivial solution in the form of sharing of model parameters which is exactly what the current work also employs. Parameter sharing comes at the expense of some drop in retrieval effectiveness.

Experimental results on CodeSearchNet dataset shows that the proposed hybrid approach gives marginal improvement in retrieval efficacy (as measured in MRR) over the baseline fast retrieval model (0.76 vs 0.74 with shared parameters and 0.77 vs 0.74 with separate models). However, this marginal improvement comes at significant increase (2.5 X to 7X) in query response time over the fast retrieval model. Compared to the slow classification model, the hybrid approach is slightly less effective (with same model size) or nearly the same (with double model size).

A key concern in the context of the proposed work is the gap (in MRR) between fast retrieval model and slow classification model is actually small - 0.74 vs 0.78. The proposed work attempts to bridge this small gap using a hybrid approach but at the cost of slower query response time. It is conceivable that future improvements in the fast retrieval model or even better parameter tuning of the current model might make the fast retrieval model as effective as the slow classification model while not losing its efficiency advantage over both the slow classification model and the hybrid approach. It might also be possible to get better retrieval efficacy by modifying the loss function suitably to boost precision. 

Some comments/questions:
Even with K = 10, the classifier phase of cascade takes significantly more time than fast encoder search. Why?
Left parenthesis is missing in Equation 1.
In Section 3, 'separat' should be corrected to 'separate'.

[1] A Cascade Ranking Model for Efficient Ranked Retrieval
http://www.jimmylin.umiacs.io/publications/Wang_etal_SIGIR2011.pdf
[2] Hashing-based Approaches to Spelling Correction of Personal Names, EMNLP 2010
https://aclanthology.org/D10-1122.pdf
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed work attempts to bridge the gap between fast retrieval models and slow classification models using a hybrid approach that uses both. However, the gap is rather small and will quite likely be bridged by enhancements to fast retrieval model by way of better parameter tuning, loss function fine tuned for the application, more data or a combination. Compared to the fast retrieval models, the proposed hybrid approach is significantly slower while providing only marginal improvement in retrieval effectiveness. Further, there is no appreciable novelty in the proposed approach.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2469 by Reviewer DPco

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for their valuable and insightful feedback. Please find our responses below.

Re: Compared to the fast retrieval models, the proposed hybrid approach is significantly slower while providing only marginal improvement in retrieval effectiveness.

We’d like to emphasize that the improvements on the semantic code search task when using the cascaded approach were observed not only on the MRR scores but also on other metrics like recall@1 (which is equivalent to the hit rate: whether or not the top result is correct) (Fig 6). 

We agree that the proposed improvement comes at the expense of higher inference duration. However this trade-off is highly subjective and one can imagine scenarios where a marginally higher MRR/hit rate can be desirable even if it comes at the cost of 3x higher inference duration (see Table 4). This is particularly valid in our case as the resulting model’s throughput in Table 4, while 3x slower than the fast method, is still reasonable (0.3 seconds for a single query) for a practical search system. This is in contrast to the slow classifier based approach, where the inference time is unreasonably long (9+ seconds for a single query). Our argument is based on the insight that with a typical search system, user queries would be dealt online (on the fly, one query at a time), with little or no scope to batch them. Existing code pre-trained transformer models when used in the cascaded fashion can lead to improvements in code search. We believe that this observation, while unsurprising, is of value given the ai research community’s recent emphasis on building developer productivity tools.

Nevertheless, we agree that in many practical scenarios, one might prefer the simpler single stage model. Given this feedback, we plan to explore further possible optimizations to parallelize the slow classifier stage of the model in order to keep the cascaded model’s throughput close to the baseline fast encoder’s. 

Re: The gap will quite likely be bridged by enhancements to the fast retrieval model by way of better parameter tuning, loss function fine tuned for the application, more data or a combination.

For a fair comparison between the hybrid, fast, and slow models, we used identical computational resources for all the variants (8 x A100 GPUs). Given the same amount of GPU RAM, the fast models actually could enjoy a higher batch size (which is known to benefit models trained with infoNCE loss) than the hybrid (shared) or slow ones, since the concatenated input would lead to higher RAM requirements (attention operation’s space complexity is quadratic in sequence length). This led to significant improvements in the fast model’s performance over what has been reported in previous works (see Table 3). Hence, we believe that our fast encoders are competitive given the current state of research. The infoNCE loss has been heavily used in previous works and is considered the best for this application.

We agree that further improvements in the fast retrieval model might be possible. However, any future improvements in the fast retrieval model are also likely to lead to improvements in the cascaded model’s performance. Particularly, cascaded models are likely to benefit if future fast models could improve their recall, as pointed out in your review. 

Besides, one could argue that many or all of the techniques mentioned - (i) better parameter tuning (ii) loss function fine-tuned for the application (iii) more data are also likely to help the slow model, along with the fast model, thus possibly leading to improvements in the fast model. We therefore see value in proposing the cascaded scheme.

Re: Even with K = 10, the classifier phase of cascade takes significantly more time than fast encoder search. Why? 

Inference with the fast encoder search involves a single forward pass for the query, while the index is ready from offline construction. For the second stage of the cascaded model with K=10, we perform forward pass on 10 input examples (10 candidates x 1 query) instead of 1 in the fast stage. While these 10 can be processed in a single batch (offering some speedup over processing 10 of them individually), their longer sequence length (query + candidate code snippet) contributes to a slower forward pass as compared to the fast encoder approach. Future work could investigate this further and propose optimizations on the second stage’s implementation to improve the inference duration.

display_title: Thanks for your detailed response to the original review

content.title: Thanks for your detailed response to the original review
content.comment:
"Existing code pre-trained transformer models when used in the cascaded fashion can lead to improvements in code search."

Sure, but this improvement comes at the expense of making retrieval significantly slower compared to the fast encoder model while the improvement in retrieval accuracy is marginal. While a response time of 0.3 second might seem acceptable for the data set used in the experimental study, it might not be so in practice when much larger data sets are used. 

"We agree that further improvements in the fast retrieval model might be possible. However, any future improvements in the fast retrieval model are also likely to lead to improvements in the cascaded model’s performance."

The point missed here is that the gap between the retrieval accuracy of  fast encoder model and slow classification model is likely to shrink with improvements in model and parameter tuning and this has the implication that the need for a hybrid model also drops down.
